title: Panel Recommends Four Lunar Sites Beyond South Pole for Crewed Missions
excerpt: A NASA-sponsored National Academies report names Bhabha Crater, Mons Hadley, the Orientale Basin and the Aristarchus Plateau as priority nonpolar destinations for short crewed sorties.
body:
• A National Academies report sponsored by NASA recommends four nonpolar sites for future crewed missions: Bhabha Crater, Mons Hadley, the Orientale Basin and the Aristarchus Plateau.
  • The report treats these sorties as complementary to, not a replacement for, NASA's planned lunar south pole base and Artemis missions.
  • Each site targets different science, from farside radio astronomy at Bhabha to volcanic samples at Aristarchus and a possible gravitational-wave observatory at Orientale.
  • The notional sorties use two astronauts and one to four spacewalks, within 2 kilometers of the lander and without a crewed rover.

A new study from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has recommended four locations for future human lunar missions beyond the moon's south pole, even as NASA focuses its Artemis program on building a base at the south pole. SpaceNews reported that the recommendations include a farside crater and an Apollo landing site, while Scientific American described the panel's case for human sorties to nonpolar regions.

The four destinations in the NASA-sponsored report, Human Exploration Across the Moon, are Bhabha Crater, Mons Hadley, the Orientale Basin and the Aristarchus Plateau. The report was produced by the Committee on Key Nonpolar Destinations across the Moon.

Context

NASA's Artemis IV mission seeks to send astronauts to the lunar south pole in 2028, and China is targeting human landings there by 2030, according to Scientific American. The south pole is prized for water ice and other resources in permanently shadowed regions. The National Academies panel argues that focus should not overlook the rest of the moon, whose geologically inactive surface, with volcanic activity ended more than a billion years ago and no plate tectonics, preserves a record of the moon's formation and of material that has struck it.

Each recommended site offers different science. Bhabha Crater, on the lunar farside, would be the farthest and most isolated location humans have ever explored, giving access to material from the moon's oldest preserved impact basin and a radio-quiet setting for radio and optical astronomy experiments shielded from Earth's emissions, the report says. Mons Hadley, on the near side near the Apollo 15 landing site, would let crews revisit hardware and biological materials exposed to the lunar environment for more than 50 years, collect new geological samples, and host a space weather observatory and a radiation-shielding experiment using piled regolith.

The Orientale Basin, on the outer edge of the moon's disk as seen from Earth, is described as the best-preserved large multi-ringed impact basin in the solar system. Crews would return samples to Earth to understand how it formed and could deploy a gravitational-wave observatory in its seismically quiet environment. The Aristarchus Plateau is a geologically rich volcanic landscape where samples could reveal volcanic processes and potentially important resources, and which could also host a space weather observatory.

Impact and Analysis

“Returning to the moon will be a great achievement for humanity—and setting foot where we never have before will be a major moment for science,” said James Day, co-chair of the committee and a professor at the University of California, San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography, in the report's release summarized by NASA Watch. Committee co-chair Daniel Dumbacher, a professor at Purdue University, said the four sites would let astronauts study questions ranging from using lunar soil to grow plants to understanding the sources of gravitational waves.

Committee member Clive Neal of the University of Notre Dame told Scientific American the exercise is meant “to be enabling for Artemis and not a distraction,” pointing to a “distributed” moon base — a network of interlinked sites providing more value than a solitary outpost. The report makes the same point formally: it treats nonpolar exploration as complementary to sustained polar exploration, and frames the question as how humans and robots can be used together, not which should explore alone.

What's Next

The report is a recommendation, not a mission schedule. Its notional sorties are deliberately modest — two astronauts, one to four extravehicular activities, no crewed rover and no extensive pre-positioned infrastructure — to show that compelling science can be done with near-term capabilities. At the same time, it calls on NASA to develop capabilities that would expand that science: traveling farther than the current 2-kilometer exploration limit, a simple unpressurized rover, instruments that survive repeated lunar day-night cycles, continuous surface communications, and a high-resolution orbital tool as a successor for reconnaissance and safety planning.

No dates or funding for missions to the four sites were announced in the report coverage. Their priority order, the National Academies notes, is based on scientific return and is not necessarily the order in which missions should fly, which will depend on experience, communications and technological readiness.
